literature.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. The Booker winner has dominated the literary pages again this week, but there are also some fine pieces on narrators, ageing novels and what to read next.

Let me begin with M John Harrison, who at eighty-one is the oldest person ever to win the Booker Prize. The Bookseller has an interview with him about age, writing and his long refusal of genre labels, and he says something rather lovely: "It's weird because I still feel twenty-six." It's candid and funny, and the sort of line your students might enjoy hearing from a prizewinning writer. The Rugby Observer, his home town paper, reports on the win as a heartening story of late recognition, which it certainly is.

The Guardian asks a bigger question: does this win mean science fiction is finally accepted by what it calls a snobby literary establishment? It points out that this is the first win for a science-fiction-leaning novel, and it gathers views from Kazuo Ishiguro and others on how prizes have treated the fantastic. If you want to place Harrison himself, The Indian Express has a clear explainer on the New Weird, the term he is associated with, and on where his unsettling fiction sits in the literary tradition. Open Magazine also has a piece on the new winner, under the headline "Catastrophic Effect: The subversive humanity of the new Booker winner". I only have the headline to go on, so I can tell you no more than that it looks at the book's tone and approach.

Now to novels and how they age. Literary Hub carries an essay by Adam Gopnik on Hemingway's The Sun Also Rises, which turns one hundred. He weighs the dated prejudices in the book against its enduring hold on readers, and writes about the Lost Generation along the way. It's a thoughtful piece on what happens to a novel as a century passes, and it could be useful for a class discussion about reading older books honestly without simply discarding them. The Paris Review, in its Daily column, looks at Barbara Trapido's debut novel forty years on. It presents the book as one about how to live, how to love and how to recover from heartbreak, and it pays attention to the threads of imagery running through it. That sounds like a fine invitation to go back to her.

On to new fiction and, in particular, narrators, which I know matter to you. The Guardian reviews Jane Schoenbrun's first novel, Public Access Afterworld. Its narrator is Bethany Peters, a trans content moderator at a company rather like YouTube, who spends her days watching disturbing material. The reviewer calls it a wry, fun descent into the dark world behind our screens, with horror flickering in the television static, and says the narrator is the strong centre of the book. The Guardian also reviews the audiobook of Ben Lerner's Transcription, read by Seth Numrich. An anxious, unnamed narrator travels to interview his former mentor, a ninety-year-old German writer, and the story becomes a layered meditation on memory, family and storytelling. The review calls it a book for the smartphone era, which makes the audio format feel quite fitting.

If you are looking for your next reads, there are several sources. The Guardian has its round-up of the best new paperbacks for November and December, with titles from Benjamin Myers, Jeanette Winterson and John Updike. It also singles out an experimental novel about a German actor and a study of how the arts can boost health, which might be pleasant to browse before the winter holidays. Literary Hub offers a list of ten great debut novels from 2026 that you might have missed. The text I have is brief and doesn't show the titles, so you would need to follow the link to see which ones it recommends. Their weekly roundup of five book reviews is more concrete. It includes M. John Harrison's The End of Everything, Tom Overton's study of John Berger, and Emily Ogden's Darkness Becomes Bright, a nice reminder that Berger's way of looking at paintings still draws attention. And in the hundredth Annotated Nightstand column, the translator Katrina Dodson talks about what she is reading now and what comes next. Her work on Brazilian literature gives it particular appeal if you enjoy thinking about language and translation.

Finally, two pieces where stories are tied to lived history. On Literary Hub, Daniel Miyares talks in a podcast about his first graphic novel, How to Say Goodbye in Cuban. He discusses immigration and Cuban history, and touches on the effects of American sanctions, so there is a small political thread, though the heart of it is a family story told in pictures. And there is a personal essay on why we should archive Black motherhood. The writer describes lacking the words to comfort her during pregnancy, and argues for why such stories need to be gathered and kept. It is a quiet, thoughtful reminder of how stories hold and console us.

That's the literary world for today, Yamuna, and I hope something in it keeps you company over a cup of tea.
literature.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. The past two days have been dominated by a Booker Prize story with a rather lovely human face, and around it there are some good pieces on narrators, on books growing old, and on the quieter business of reading and translating.

Let me begin with the prize. M John Harrison has become the oldest person ever to win the Booker, at eighty-one. The Bookseller has an interview in which he talks about age, writing, and his long refusal of genre labels, and the line everyone is quoting is a wonderfully disarming one: "It's weird because I still feel twenty-six." There is something quite touching in that, coming from a writer receiving the highest honour in English-language fiction at an age when many people assume the story is over. If you ever want a candid, unpompous voice to put in front of students on the subject of writing and ageing, this feels like a good one. The Rugby Observer, meanwhile, has taken the local-pride route, noting that the oldest ever Booker winner was born in Rugby. It is a small piece, but it is a heartening story of late recognition, and it is pleasing to see a hometown paper claim him.

The bigger conversation is about what the win means. The Guardian asks whether this is science fiction finally being accepted by what it calls a snobby literary establishment. The piece points out that this is the first Booker win for a novel leaning towards science fiction, and it reflects on the long divide in literary publishing between the so-called serious and the fantastic. Kazuo Ishiguro is among those who weigh in, which is interesting in itself, since Ishiguro has often moved between registers and has not always been comfortable with the walls people build between them. It is a useful article if you want to show older students how prizes quietly define what counts as literature, and how those definitions shift.

To place Harrison himself, The Indian Express has an explainer on the New Weird, the term he is associated with. It is a helpful primer on a kind of fiction that is unsettling and unusual, a blend of the strange and the literary that does not sit comfortably in either camp. If you are not already familiar with his work, it gives you a way into the tradition he belongs to. And Open Magazine has a short piece on the new Booker winner under the headline "Catastrophic Effect", which speaks of the subversive humanity of the novel. I should be honest that only the headline was available to me, so I cannot say much more than that the piece points to a book whose tone is both disruptive and humane, a combination that sounds well worth the reading. Alongside all this, Literary Hub's weekly round-up of five reviews includes a review of Harrison's book The End of Everything, so there is plenty of critical attention to follow if you want to go deeper.

Now to narrators, which I know is where your heart sits. The Guardian has two reviews this week that are, in different ways, all about voice.

The first is of Jane Schoenbrun's first novel, Public Access Afterworld. Schoenbrun is better known for film, but this is prose, and the book follows Bethany Peters, a trans content moderator at a company much like YouTube. Her job is to watch disturbing material so that the rest of us do not have to. The reviewer calls it a wry, fun descent into the dark world behind our screens, with horror seeping in through the television static, and it sounds as though Bethany is a strong narrator at the centre of it, someone whose dry humour is both a defence and a way of looking. If you enjoy a thriller with a distinctive voice, and with something to say about how we look at things, this might be one to note down.

The second is a review of the audiobook of Ben Lerner's Transcription, narrated by Seth Numrich. The reviewer describes it as a meditation on memory for the smartphone era. An unnamed, anxious narrator travels to interview his former mentor, a ninety-year-old German writer, and the story folds in memory, family and the act of storytelling itself. What is intriguing is the format. A narrator who is anxious, self-questioning and unnamed seems to ask to be heard rather than read, and the review suggests that the audio version has its own particular pleasures. For someone who spends her days thinking about how voices carry meaning, that might be worth a listen on one of those drives down into the Grésivaudan.

That brings me to the pieces looking backwards, which I think you will enjoy, as they are about how books live on.

In Literary Hub, Adam Gopnik revisits Hemingway's The Sun Also Rises on the hundredth anniversary of its publication. His essay is called "An Ode to the Lost Generation", and it weighs the novel's dated prejudices against its enduring hold on readers. That tension is exactly the sort of thing a good classroom discussion can be built on. How do we read a book that we know has aged badly in places, and yet which still pulls us in? Gopnik takes the Lost Generation seriously, those restless young people drifting around postwar Paris and Spain, and he asks how a novel ages, rather than simply whether it has. It is a thoughtful, generous essay rather than a takedown or a defence, and it connects to your interest in novels that teach history better than history essays do, since the mood of that postwar world is almost the point of the book.

The Paris Review's Daily has a retrospective on Barbara Trapido's debut novel, forty years after it was published. The piece frames the book as being about how to live, love and recover from heartbreak, and it is described as a book of threads of imagery, which suggests something patterned and carefully woven rather than simply plotted. If you do not already know Trapido, this might be a gentle invitation. The emphasis on narrators and emotional truth feels right for you, and it is the sort of novel that might suit a first-year sixth form reader who wants something intelligent and warm.

Also in that reflective vein, the Literary Hub round-up of five reviews mentions Tom Overton's study of John Berger and Emily Ogden's Darkness Becomes Bright. I only have the titles, so I will not pretend to describe them in detail. But a new study of Berger is of course of interest given your fondness for the links between painting and writing. Berger is, after all, the great modern guide to looking at pictures in words, and a fresh look at his work is welcome.

On the reading-list side of things, there are three pieces that might help you plan.

Literary Hub's Annotated Nightstand column has reached its hundredth edition, and this time the guest is the translator Katrina Dodson, who talks about what she is reading now and what she plans to read next. Her work on Brazilian literature makes this a natural fit for someone who cares about how language travels between cultures. A translator's reading list is always an interesting thing, because they read with an ear for sentences in a way that most of us do not.

Also from Literary Hub, a piece on ten great debut novels you might have missed in 2026. I will be straightforward: the text I had was brief and the list itself was not visible, so I cannot give you titles. But it is there for you to explore if you are looking for fresh fiction that has slipped under the radar.

And The Guardian has its round-up of the best new paperbacks for November and December, with names including Benjamin Myers, Jeanette Winterson and John Updike. Two things in it caught my attention: an experimental novel about a German actor, and a study of how the arts can improve our health. That second one might be a good conversation starter in a lesson on why we read and make art at all. Paperbacks are, of course, a good moment for a bookshop browse, and the weeks before Christmas are a nice time to be doing it, perhaps with a stop at a market in Grenoble.

I will end with two pieces about stories as a form of keeping and consoling, which sit a little apart from the rest.

Literary Hub has a conversation with Daniel Miyares about his first graphic novel, How to Say Goodbye in Cuban. It is a podcast, and it covers immigration and Cuban history, and also touches on the effects of American sanctions, so there is a small political thread, though the heart of it is the story of leaving and the family history behind it. A graphic novel for a literature teacher is an interesting object, since it carries both image and word, and history is told through a personal lens. It might be a good text to set beside prose accounts of migration in your classes.

The last item is a personal essay, also from Literary Hub, called "What We Lose When We Don't Archive Black Motherhood". The writer describes the absence of words to comfort her during pregnancy, the sense of reaching for a book or a story and finding nothing that matched her experience, and why it matters to record and keep those stories. It is a thoughtful piece about how literature holds and consoles us, and about what happens when it is not there. I think it sits well with much of what you value in fiction, the idea that a story is something one can step into and be sheltered by.

So, a week in which an eighty-one-year-old feels twenty-six, a hundred-year-old novel still argues with its readers, and a good many new books wait on the nightstand. I hope you find a quiet hour to enjoy a few of them.

art.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. Today's art news has a pleasing shape: a few quiet things close to home, then a run of painters' lives, and a good deal where art meets books and music.

Starting nearby. L'Essentiel reports a new exhibition at the Musée de Grenoble, though all I have is the headline, so I can't tell you the artists, the dates or the theme. It's worth a look at the museum's own listings before the weekend. L'Essentiel also has a piece on calligraphy appearing on the Place de Gordes in Grenoble, again with little more than the headline, but it sounds like the kind of small, public intervention that makes a square worth crossing. Down in Fontaine, jds.fr lists an exhibition from the Atelier Eugénie Fauny, with dates, hours and prices on the listing, though I only have the title line to go on. And in Mens, Le Dauphiné Libéré reports that the museum is showing creations by nursery-school pupils. I rather like that: very young children's work given a proper place on a museum wall. Finally, Actu.fr says a work from the Fête des Lumières in Lyon is coming to Isère, and the piece gives the where and when. The text I have is thin, so do check the article for the details, but it's a public artwork not far from you.

Now to the lives behind the paintings, which seems to be the theme of the day. In Metz, the first international retrospective of Séraphine Louis has opened, according to Beaux Arts Magazine. She lived from eighteen sixty-four to nineteen forty-two, taught herself to paint, and worked as a cleaner. The exhibition sets out to show the great painter behind the legend, so she is seen on her own terms rather than as a curiosity. It's a story that would make a fine novel, and in a way it already has.

In Paris, the same magazine reports that Catherine Hiegel is playing Suzanne Valadon at the Théâtre Montparnasse. The play is set in nineteen thirty-five, three years before Valadon's death, so it catches her late, looking back. Painting and theatre together, with a very fine actress. And Hyperallergic reviews a new documentary on Romare Bearden, the collage artist. The reviewer finds the best moments are the ones where we simply watch people meeting his work, which feels right for an artist who built pictures out of fragments of other lives.

Now the crossing between art, fiction and music, which I suspect is your favourite territory. BBC Radio 4's Front Row has a review of Jonathan Coe's novel Lessons in Harmony, about the friendship between Ravel and Vaughan Williams. The same programme covers the Inside Bloomsbury exhibition at Tate Britain, on Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant. So in one episode you get a novel about two composers and a show about two painters, all of it about friendship and the way artists shape one another. It would make good listening on a walk up to Les Adrets.

For a different way of looking at a famous picture, Hyperallergic reports that scientists have found Rembrandt's Night Watch is home to teeming microbes. They hope this invisible life will help explain some of the painting's mysteries. It's a strange and rather wonderful thought: that one of the most studied canvases in the world is, in a sense, still alive.

Also in London, the National Gallery has published a three-part film series today called Linked Lives: Art and Empire. It looks at how the gallery's early history was shaped by empire and colonialism, drawing on Dr Sean Cham's research into the people behind the paintings, including enslaved people who are so often left out of institutional history. For anyone who likes to learn history through stories, it seems a thoughtful way into the subject, and perhaps useful for a lesson on how a painting can hold more than what's on its surface.

Last, a run of photography, mostly from The Guardian. The first is a piece on Jill Posener, whose witty, feminist photographs from the nineteen eighties answered misogyny and Thatcherite conservatism. Among them is a graffitied billboard she photographed on London's Farringdon Road in nineteen seventy-nine. A retrospective now marks fifty years of her work, and the article is carried by her own words. She says she railed against the stereotype of the humourless lesbian, and humour was her weapon of choice.

In New York, the Metropolitan Museum of Art has A Long Shadow, which runs until the second of May, twenty twenty-seven. It brings together fifteen artists, with prints, books, magazines and a video installation, to show how Japanese photographers documented postwar Japan, from punks to sex workers to a society in transition. The Guardian notes it is the first show of Japanese photography at the Met in over thirty years.

Two lighter pieces to finish. One is a photo essay in which Teddy Trevor, now ninety, remembers the Australian sideshow tradition of his family and fellow showmen. The voices are vivid, and it reads like a piece of oral history, with characters you could happily meet in a novel. The other is a collection of retro holiday guides gathered by Jonny Trunk, who, rather touchingly, never went on holiday as a child. The graphic design is lovely, and there's a gentle, nostalgic idealism in every cover.

That's the art for today, Yamuna; may your morning have a little more colour than the weather suggests.
art.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's a gentle Friday for art news, with a few small things close to home, some fine stories of painters and the lives behind them, and a handful of photographs to end on.

Let me begin nearby, since the local items are the ones you might actually act on. The first is the most promising and, frustratingly, the thinnest. L'Essentiel announces a new exhibition at the Musée de Grenoble. All I have is the headline, so I can't tell you the artists, the dates or the theme. But when the museum announces something new, it's usually worth a look, so it may be worth checking the museum's own pages before the weekend. I'll keep an eye out for fuller details as they appear.

Also in Grenoble, L'Essentiel reports that calligraphy is making its way onto the Place de Gordes. Again, the text is only a headline, so I can't say who is behind it or how long it will stay. But there's something pleasing about writing, which is after all your own territory, turned into a public image on a city square. If you're passing through the centre, it might be a nice thing to stumble upon.

A little further out, a listing on jds.fr gives dates, opening hours and prices for an exhibition at the Atelier Eugénie Fauny in Fontaine. The details I have are only what the title line shows, so the specifics are for you to look up. But Fontaine is an easy hop from the valley, and small studio exhibitions are often the ones with the most personality.

And then there's a lovely story from Mens, in the Isère. Le Dauphiné Libéré reports that the museum there is showing creations by nursery-school pupils. I like this one very much. It gives very young children's work a proper place on a museum's walls, rather than a corridor or a classroom noticeboard. As a teacher, you'll know how much it means to a child to see their own work given that kind of dignity.

One more Isère item, with a Lyon connection. Actu.fr says that a work from the Fête des Lumières in Lyon is coming to the Isère, and that its article explains where and when you can see it. The text I have is thin and doesn't give those details, so do look at the piece itself. A public light work travelling from Lyon to our own department is an appealing prospect as the evenings draw in.

Now to the stories of painters, and here the connections with literature are strongest.

The one I'd put first is from Metz, where, according to Beaux Arts Magazine, the first international retrospective of Séraphine Louis has just opened. She lived from eighteen sixty-four to nineteen forty-two, and she was a self-taught painter who had worked as a cleaner. The magazine's headline says the exhibition reveals the great painter behind the legend. That phrase is interesting, because the legend has often been the way into her story: the humble woman, the cleaner who painted. A retrospective of this kind is a chance to see the work on its own terms rather than through the myth. It's very much a story of an overlooked artist finally being looked at properly, and it has the shape of a novel, which I think you'd appreciate. It might also make a good starting point for a conversation with older pupils about who gets remembered, and how.

Staying with painters and storytelling, Beaux Arts Magazine also writes about the Théâtre Montparnasse in Paris, where the great actress Catherine Hiegel plays the painter Suzanne Valadon. The play is set in nineteen thirty-five, three years before Valadon's death. So we meet her late in life, looking back, presumably, though I only know the setting and not the plot. Still, it's a pleasing meeting of painting and theatre, and Hiegel is a name that carries weight on the French stage. If you're in Paris at some point, it could be a rewarding evening.

Then, from across the Channel, a Front Row programme on BBC Radio 4 that seems made for you. It reviews Jonathan Coe's novel Lessons in Harmony, which is about the friendship between Ravel and Vaughan Williams. Two composers, two countries, one friendship: that is a lovely premise for fiction, and Coe is a writer with a gift for warmth and comic timing, though I'll let you be the judge of how that plays out here. The same programme looks at the Inside Bloomsbury exhibition at Tate Britain, devoted to Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant. So within one half-hour you get a novel about music and an exhibition about painters, which is almost a lesson plan in how the arts speak to one another. It's also a decent listen if you want something for the journey down the valley.

There's a thread running through these three. Each one is about a person, and about the difficulty of seeing a person clearly through the work they leave behind. That leads me to the next group, which is about documentaries and the lives behind well-known pictures.

Hyperallergic reviews a new documentary about Romare Bearden, the collage artist. The reviewer finds that the best moments come when we watch people engaging with his work. I think that's a shrewd observation. A film about an artist can easily become a parade of dates and talking heads, but there's something much more alive in watching a person stand in front of a collage and really look. Since you enjoy documentaries, and especially the sort that make you feel the connection between art and life, this one sounds worth tracking down.

From the National Gallery in London comes a film series in three parts, called Linked Lives: Art and Empire, published today on YouTube. It examines how the early history of the gallery was shaped by empire and colonialism. It draws on the research of Doctor Sean Cham, who has looked into the lives behind the paintings, including enslaved people who are often left out of institutional history. What I find compelling is the idea of asking not only what a painting shows, but who stood behind it, who paid for it, and who is missing from the record. I think this is the sort of history that novels often do better than essays, by giving a voice to those the archives overlooked. And for your classroom, it could be a good bridge between a painting, a historical question, and a text. It's three parts, so you can dip in at your leisure.

And one for the more curious among us. Hyperallergic reports that scientists have found that Rembrandt's Night Watch is home to teeming microbes. The hope is that this invisible life might help explain some of the painting's mysteries. I like that the story invites us to look again at one of the most famous canvases in the world, and to realise that even a painting we think we know is still, in a quiet way, alive. I can't tell you what the mysteries are, as the summary doesn't say, but it's a striking image to carry around: a masterpiece, seen by thousands, with a hidden population living on its surface.

Now, to finish, photography, which seems to be the art of the day in The Guardian's art and design pages.

First, Jill Posener. The Guardian's piece is built around her own words, and the headline quotes her: she railed against the stereotype of the humourless lesbian. Her photographs from the nineteen eighties are witty and feminist, and they answered the misogyny and the Thatcherite conservatism of the time. One of them is a graffitied billboard that she shot on Farringdon Road in London in nineteen seventy-nine. A retrospective now marks fifty years of her work. What I like here is the stress on humour as a tool, as a way of getting a serious point across with a smile. It's a good reminder that satire, in pictures or in prose, can be both generous and sharp.

Next, in New York, an exhibition at the Metropolitan Museum of Art called A Long Shadow. It runs from this year until the second of May, twenty twenty-seven, and brings together fifteen artists, with prints, books, magazines and a video installation. Its subject is how Japanese photographers documented postwar Japan, and The Guardian's picture gallery gives a taste of it, with punks, sex workers and a society in transition. It's the first show of Japanese photography at the Met in over thirty years, which is quite a gap. Even if New York is a long way off, the pictures online are worth a look, and the long run of the show gives plenty of time should a trip ever come up.

Then two lighter pieces, both from The Guardian, and both about a vanished world of printed and spoken things. The first is a photo essay in which Teddy Trevor, who is now ninety, recalls the Australian sideshow tradition of his family and fellow showmen. The headline captures the patter: hurry, hurry, get your tickets now. He is described as the last of the great Australian showmen, and the piece is carried by the voices and vivid characters. It's oral history of a very lively kind, and the sort of thing you could imagine sitting alongside a novel about travelling performers.

The second is a collection of retro holiday guides, vintage brochures gathered by Jonny Trunk, who, rather touchingly, never went on holiday as a child. So there's a little melancholy tucked inside the nostalgia, and I think that's what makes it interesting. The graphic design, with its bright, idealised promises of sun and sea, is a pleasure in itself, and it might be fun to think of those brochures as a kind of fiction too, with their own narrators and their own versions of paradise.

So, to gather it up. Closer to home there are several small things to watch for: the new show at the Musée de Grenoble, the calligraphy on the Place de Gordes, the studio exhibition in Fontaine, the Lumières work heading into the Isère, and the nursery-school pupils in Mens. For stories, there's the long-awaited retrospective of Séraphine Louis in Metz, Catherine Hiegel as Valadon in Paris, and Coe's novel and the Bloomsbury exhibition on Front Row. And for looking again, there's Bearden on film, the lives behind the National Gallery's paintings, and the unseen life on the Night Watch.

That's the art for today, Yamuna, and I hope something in it sends you off looking at a painting, or a billboard, a little differently this weekend.

around.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's Friday the thirteenth of November, and the last couple of days have brought a gentle mix of music, memory and early winter bustle to your corner of the Alps.

Let me begin with the music, since there's an organ in it. This Saturday, the fourteenth of November, there's a concert of Bach at the Saint-Joseph church in Grenoble, announced by Le Dauphiné Libéré. Grenoble Mag also writes about the organist Michel Alleysson, who sets Bach in conversation with Italian music at the Saint-Joseph organ. That piece gives no date, so I can't promise it's the same programme, but the church and the organ are the same, and it seems a reasonable guess. Either way, a Saturday of Bach in a Grenoble church sounds like a good way to spend an evening.

Now to exhibitions and stories of the past. In Chambéry, there's an exhibition of Albanian portraits, described by Unidivers as the faces a dictatorship wanted to erase. The text is short, so I can't say much about the works themselves, but it promises history told through faces, which is rather your territory: memory, art and the stubborn survival of people someone tried to remove from the record.

A little further north-west, in the Chartreuse hills, Isère Attractivité lists a free exhibition called "Hier, au temps futur", or "Yesterday, in the future tense". It opens today at Le Sappey-en-Chartreuse and runs until the thirtieth of January. I don't have details of what's on show, but it's a long run, so it could suit a slow winter afternoon with a walk either side.

And in a similar spirit, there's a story from France 3 Alpes about the Great War. A woman from Isère, the great-granddaughter of a poilu who was interned in a psychiatric hospital after the fighting, is writing in order to give him back his voice. The title of the piece is striking: "these men afflicted with women's illnesses". It's a reminder of how the psychological toll of nineteen fourteen to eighteen was misunderstood and, often, silenced. It reads like the kind of family history that could easily become a novel.

On the technology side of culture, there's a virtual reality experience called Insider-outsider at the Saint-Exupéry media library in Montbonnot-Saint-Martin. It's today, the thirteenth, at five in the afternoon. The listing is sparse, so I can't tell you more, but it's very close to home if you're curious.

Now for the weekend on stage. The Journal des Entreprises' leisure pages, jds.fr, have published two roundups for the thirteenth to the fifteenth of November: ten ideas across Isère and nine for Grenoble itself. Among them are a ballet, which I'd guess is the one to catch your eye, a much-awaited indie rock concert by Girls In Hawaii, and, for the more adventurous, canyoning in the Vercors. There's also a mini-golf course styled on a prison, which sounds delightfully eccentric. The summaries I have don't name the ballet company or the venue, so it's worth checking the full lists.

Theatre is also having a moment. Grenoble Mag reports that the Festival international de théâtre action is back, with eight socially engaged new productions running until the twenty-fifth of November. I don't have details of the individual pieces, but the festival has a serious, committed focus, so it may suit an evening when you want something with a bit of bite.

Circus fans haven't been forgotten. Le Dauphiné Libéré has published a guide to the Festival du cirque in Grenoble, covering the acts, the jury and the staging. The snippet I have gives no dates, so it's worth looking at the article itself, but it's a live spectacle close to home.

There's one more concert, with a gentler purpose. Ici-Grenoble announces an open-air concert by Musique aux frontières, in support of exiled people. No date or venue came through in the text, I'm afraid, but it's one to keep an eye on if you like music with a human cause behind it.

Finally, some seasonal and down-to-earth news. Grenoble's Christmas market opens on the twentieth of November, according to mesinfos, and Grenoble Mag has published the dates and opening hours for this year. I only have the headline of that piece, so the exact times will need a look on their site. But with the opening a week away, you can start planning a wander through the stalls.

On the producers' side, the Département de l'Isère has a piece called "Huile de noix de Tencin: l'or du vieux moulin", about walnut oil from an old mill in Tencin, which is very near Les Adrets. The text is brief, but it's a lovely local story about a product with real character, and walnut oil seems to belong to this time of year, with the first cold days and bowls of salad or warm bread.

And to end on something hopeful, Ici-Grenoble reports that an orchard is being planted at the Université autogérée de Grenoble, the self-managed university. There's no more detail than that, but there's something nice about trees going into the ground just as the weather turns.

So that's your local round-up: Bach in a church, faces rescued from erasure, a poilu finding his voice, and walnut oil from a mill down the road. Have a lovely Friday, Yamuna.
around.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's Friday the thirteenth of November, and the last couple of days have left a pleasantly full shelf of things happening close to home, with a good deal of music, a little theatre and dance, some memory and history, and the first signs of winter festivities.

Let me begin with the music, since that's where the firmest date is. On Saturday the fourteenth of November, at the church of Saint-Joseph in Grenoble, there's an organ concert of Bach. Le Dauphiné Libéré announced it. Grenoble Mag, meanwhile, has a piece about the organist Michel Alleysson, who is programming Bach alongside Italian music at the Saint-Joseph organ. That second piece gives no date in what I have, so I can't promise it's the very same evening, but the church, the instrument and the composer all line up, and it seems quite likely they describe the same recital. If so, it's an interesting programme. Bach is so often heard on his own, in that grave, architectural way, and here he's set in conversation with Italian music, which is the tradition he himself admired and borrowed from. I'd suggest checking the time and ticket details with the church or the newspaper before you go, as I don't have them. But for a Saturday in November, an organ in a Grenoble church is a lovely way to spend an hour or two, and if you like music that fills a whole space and seems to make the stone itself resonate, it's well worth it.

There's another concert with a different spirit. Ici-Grenoble reports an outdoor concert by an ensemble called Musique aux frontières, held in support of exiled people. I'm afraid the announcement as I have it gives neither a date nor a venue, so this one is a thing to look up rather than to plan around just yet. But I wanted you to know about it, because the idea is a good one: music offered as a gesture of welcome, in the open air, for people who have had to leave their homes. It's the kind of event that sits well with the stories you love, where art and human circumstance meet.

And for something quite different, the weekend roundups from jds.fr mention a concert by Girls In Hawaii, the indie rock group, described as much anticipated. That is probably not your first choice of the weekend, but it's the sort of evening that fills a room in Grenoble, so you may hear about it on Monday from a pupil or two.

That brings me to the stage. The same roundup from jds.fr, which covers Isère from the thirteenth to the fifteenth of November, lists a ballet among its ten ideas, and the Grenoble-specific version, with nine suggestions, includes it too. The listings I have don't say which company or which piece, so I can't tell you more than that, but of everything on the weekend lists, the ballet is the one I'd put first for you, given your fondness for dance. The same lists include some less likely options, such as canyoning in the Vercors, which in mid-November sounds bracing, and a mini-golf course styled after Alcatraz, a prison-themed course I will leave entirely to your discretion.

Staying with performance, Grenoble Mag tells us that the Festival international de théâtre action is back, with eight socially engaged new productions, running until the twenty-fifth of November. So there's still a good stretch of time to catch something. The text I have says little about the individual pieces, but the idea behind theatre action is theatre that takes up real questions of society and speaks to them directly. It's a serious festival, and if you like drama that has something to say as well as something to show, it could be a good source of an evening out, and perhaps even of ideas for your classes. I'd look at the programme to see which of the eight creations appeals.

There's also the Festival du cirque in Grenoble. Le Dauphiné Libéré has published a guide to it, covering the acts, the jury and the staging. The piece as I have it doesn't give dates, so I can't say when it takes place, but it's one to look for if you fancy something lighter and more spectacular, perhaps with a friend or a visiting relative. Circus has a way of being both athletic and poetic, and a jury suggests a proper competition, with performers pushing themselves.

Now to the quieter side of the week: exhibitions, memory and history, which I suspect will interest you most.

In Chambéry, Unidivers reports on an exhibition of Albanian portraits, called "Icônes d'Albanie", with the subtitle about faces that the dictatorship wanted to erase. The text is short, and I don't have dates or the venue, but the idea is striking. Icons, painted faces, and a regime that tried to wipe them out. It's history told through images, and that's exactly the territory where paintings and written works start to speak to each other. If you go, I'd be curious to know whether it brings to mind any novels of that region, or the way fiction sometimes preserves what officialdom tries to delete. It would also be a good excuse for a trip to Chambéry, which is within easy reach.

Closer to the hills, there's an exhibition called "Hier, au temps futur", which opened today, the thirteenth of November, at Le Sappey-en-Chartreuse and runs until the thirtieth of January, 2027. Isère Attractivité lists it, and it's free. I don't have any description of what's in it beyond the title, which is intriguing in itself, yesterday in the future tense, almost a grammar puzzle you might enjoy. With a run of nearly three months, you needn't rush. It could suit a slow winter afternoon in the Chartreuse, perhaps with a walk beforehand if the weather is kind.

And at Montbonnot-Saint-Martin, today at five o'clock in the afternoon, the Saint Exupéry media library is offering a virtual reality experience called Insider-outsider, listed by Le Grésivaudan. The listing gives very little more, so I can't tell you what it's about, but the title suggests something to do with belonging and being on the margins. It's today, so it would be a last-minute plan, but it's in the valley, close to you, if you happen to be passing that way this evening.

I'd also like to mention a story from France 3 Alpes, in Isère, which isn't an event but which I think will speak to you. It's about a woman, the great-granddaughter of a poilu from the First World War who was interned in a psychiatric hospital, and she is writing in order to give him back his voice. The title of the piece quotes a phrase of the time, "ces hommes atteints de maladies de femmes", these men afflicted with women's illnesses, which tells you a great deal about how the suffering of soldiers was misunderstood and dismissed. It's family history, and it's the forgotten psychological cost of the war of 1914 to 1918, and it's the sort of material that novels do so well, bringing a single life up close and letting it carry a whole period's weight. If you're teaching anything on the war poets or on fiction about the Great War, this could be a lovely, very local counterpoint, a voice from Isère rather than from the trenches of fiction.

Now to seasonal and local life, because the winter calendar is starting to appear.

Two sources, Grenoble Mag and mesinfos, tell us that Grenoble's Christmas market for 2026 opens on the twentieth of November, that is next Friday. Grenoble Mag has an article with the dates and opening hours, but I only have the headline, so for the precise times you'll want to check the article itself. Still, the opening date is clear, and it gives you a week to decide whether you'd like to go early, before the crowds, perhaps on a weekday evening when the lights are on and the air is cold.

For something a little more rooted in the land, the Département de l'Isère has a piece called "Huile de noix de Tencin: l'or du vieux moulin", about walnut oil from an old mill in Tencin, which is quite close to Les Adrets. The text I have is brief, so I can't tell you about opening times or where to buy it, but the title itself is rather beautiful, calling the oil the gold of the old mill. The Grésivaudan and its walnuts go together, and a producer's story like this is a nice reminder of what the valley does well. If you like producers' markets, it might be worth asking after this oil next time you're out, and it would make a fine thing to cook with or to give at Christmas.

And finally, a gentle piece of good news. Ici-Grenoble reports that an orchard is being planted at the Université autogérée de Grenoble, the self-managed university. There's no more detail in what I have, but there's something heartening about planting fruit trees at this time of year, a gesture towards a future that will take years to bear fruit, quite literally. It's a small story, but a hopeful one, and it fits the season, since autumn and early winter are when trees go into the ground.

So, to put it all together for the coming days. If you want a fixed point, Saturday evening's Bach in Grenoble is it. If you want something to dip into more slowly, "Hier, au temps futur" at Le Sappey will be there until the end of January, and the Albanian icons in Chambéry offer a thoughtful outing, once you've checked the dates. The ballet, the theatre action festival and the circus are there for when you want a night of performance, and the Christmas market begins next Friday. And in between, you have a great-grandfather in Isère whose voice is being returned to him, which is a good story to carry with you.

Wherever you end up this weekend, I hope there's a good organ chord, a warm drink and a bit of Belledonne light along the way.

bfi.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's a Hamlet-heavy couple of days in the BFI corner, with some good Welsh news, a few Atwood and Angelou ideas for the oral, and a couple of reflections on reading and writing to finish.

Let me begin with Hamlet, since it's on the session twenty twenty-seven list and four pieces landed at once. The most moving is a BBC inside story about Ian Charleson, who played Hamlet on stage while dying of Aids. The headline quotes the phrase "a hell of a thing to take on", and the piece is about how a role can take on enormous personal weight. For a class studying a play so full of mortality, and of an actor-prince who watches himself perform grief, it could make a quietly powerful way into the question of what it means to inhabit Hamlet.

Then there's the Thom Yorke production, Hamlet Hail to the Thief, a collision of Shakespeare and Radiohead. The Times reviewed it at the Barbican and calls it a taut collision between the Bard and the band. The Guardian's Alexis Petridis is more mixed: he says it could have been rotten, but that it redeems what he calls Radiohead's "record that got away". Two critics, two slightly different temperatures, which is rather useful if you want older pupils to weigh up competing reviews of the same adaptation.

The fourth is a review of Raoul Bhaneja's one-man show, Hamlet (solo), where the headline praises the actor's talent. The review text is brief, but the idea of a single performer carrying every voice in the play is a lovely prompt about interpretation. Who is Hamlet when he is also Claudius, Gertrude and Ophelia?

Staying with the stage, and with 2027 texts, there are two smaller items. Florida Weekly has a piece on love and deception in The Rivals. The text is short, so it's probably a review or feature, but it's a reminder of how well Sheridan's comedy of mistaken identities and romantic scheming can work for seconde or première. And a school note: Chatham High School's theatre company is staging Twelfth Night from the nineteenth to the twenty-first of November, according to TAPinto. There's no more detail, but it's a pleasant sign of Shakespeare being played by teenagers, which is a good thing to mention to your own pupils.

Now some good news from Wales, which I thought you'd enjoy. Under Milk Wood is on the twenty twenty-seven programme, and the Tenby Observer reports that major investment has been secured for the Dylan Thomas Boathouse in Laugharne. Swansea Bay News adds the detail: seventy-seven thousand pounds is being spent, and the Boathouse will be closed until the new year. It's the place where Thomas wrote, so it's an evocative link for a class, and perhaps a reason to plan a visit once it reopens, or to show pupils photographs of the estuary setting while you read the play's opening aloud. That "to begin at the beginning" voice, with its musical, sea-washed language, is exactly the sort of writing you love to share.

Next, the oral themes. Starting with Maya Angelou, The Times of India has a piece on her habit of renting hotel rooms simply in order to write, an unusual routine for concentrating. It's author context for I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings, and a good classroom hook: pupils often assume writers work in glamorous inspiration, and here is a very practical, almost austere discipline. You could ask them where they would go to write, and why.

On Atonement, IndulgExpress looks at the famous green gown from the film, explaining how it was designed to symbolise envy and longing. That's a neat bridge between costume and McEwan's imagery. Colour, desire and jealousy matter greatly in the novel, so it could open a discussion of how an image on screen translates, or fails to translate, what the prose does with Briony's perspective. It also connects to your interest in the links between visual art and literature.

Then two Atwood items. The Miami Herald reports that Jess Gibson, Margaret Atwood's daughter, is talking about her first book with her mother at the Miami Book Fair. The detail is thin, but it offers an author-focused angle on Atwood's family and writing life, for anyone teaching The Handmaid's Tale. And Sesaya Arts Magazine reviews King Theatre Company's stage production of Alias Grace, saying it makes room for uncertainty. That seems fitting, since Grace Marks is one of fiction's great ambiguous narrators, and a stage version has to decide how much to let the audience doubt her. It's a useful discussion point about historical narrators, and about what changes when a voice that lives on the page is given a body on stage.

Finally, three pieces about reading and writing more generally, none tied to the programme but all rewarding. The Irish Independent has an interview with the novelist Yiyun Li, who says she reads War and Peace and Moby-Dick every year, and has done so for nearly twenty years. It's a lovely testimony to rereading, and might be worth quoting to pupils who feel one reading of a text is enough. Times Now reports that a Booker Prize victory has revived the debate about whether literary fiction needs to be realistic. I only have the headline and summary, but the question touches on narrative craft and would pair well with discussion of unreliable or unusual narrators. And The Guardian reviews One for Sorrow by Favel Parrett, calling it an affecting novel that builds to a devastating climax. I only have the headline, so I can't say more, but it might be one for your own reading pile.

That's the corner for today, Yamuna, and I hope something here finds its way into a lesson or onto your bedside table.
bfi.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's a Hamlet-heavy day in the BFI corner, with a good deal of Shakespeare on stage, some welcome news from Laugharne, and a few author stories that might be useful for your oral themes.

Let me start with Hamlet, since it has been busy. The piece I'd put first is from the BBC, an inside story with the headline "A hell of a thing to take on". It tells how Ian Charleson played Hamlet on stage while he was dying of Aids. I'd tread carefully with how much of it to bring into a classroom, but it speaks directly to the play you have on the 2027 programme. It is about how a role can take on enormous personal weight, when an actor is speaking lines about mortality, about what happens after death, and about readiness, while living a version of those questions himself. The BBC piece is a story about performance, but it is also a way into a question your première students may enjoy: does knowing who is speaking a line change what the line means? You could set it beside a speech such as "To be, or not to be" and ask whether a text stays fixed while its meaning moves depending on who delivers it, and when.

Alongside that, there are two reviews of the same new production, which is a rather different take on the play. It is called Hamlet Hail to the Thief, a collision of Shakespeare and Radiohead, with Thom Yorke involved, and it has been staged at the Barbican. The Times reviews it under the headline "the Bard and Radiohead's taut collision", which sounds like a warm verdict, and the word taut suggests the two worlds have been pulled tightly together rather than just placed side by side. The Guardian's Alexis Petridis is a little more mixed in his framing. His headline says it could have been rotten, but that it redeems what he calls Radiohead's "record that got away". So you have two critics, one admiring and one admiring with reservations, writing about the same night of theatre and music. I find that quite useful for teaching, because it is a ready-made exercise in comparing two reviews. Which words reveal the critic's attitude? Where does each one hedge? What does "could have been rotten" do to a reader's expectations before the praise arrives? It also gives you a modern example of a very old habit, which is writers taking Hamlet and bending it to their own purposes. If any of your students listen to Radiohead, it may be a surprisingly warm door into a play they may think of as distant.

The third Hamlet item is a review of Raoul Bhaneja's one-man show, Hamlet (solo), from the site front mezz junkies. The headline praises the actor's talent, and says the production puts it to the test. The text I have is brief, so I can't tell you much about how he handles the staging. But the idea itself is a good one for class. One actor, many characters: what do you gain, and what do you lose? A solo Hamlet forces the question of how much of the play happens inside the prince's head. You could ask students to take a short scene, say the conversation with Gertrude or the encounter with Ophelia, and imagine it performed by one voice, deciding which gestures or changes of tone would mark each speaker. That is a lovely exercise in close reading disguised as theatre.

Now some good news, and from your own region of imagination, if not your own mountains. There are two reports on the Dylan Thomas Boathouse in Laugharne. The Tenby Observer says major investment has been secured for it. The Swansea Bay News adds some detail: the Boathouse is closed until the new year, and £77,000 is being spent on it. The Boathouse is a place where Thomas wrote, which makes it a particularly evocative link to Under Milk Wood, which is on the 2027 session. I like this news for a simple reason. It is a literary place being looked after, and the closure is a short pause rather than a loss. For class, it could be an opening for a short session on how place shapes writing. Under Milk Wood is so full of voices, of a whole town heard through the night, and students often find it easier to approach once they have a sense of where it came from: a small Welsh town on an estuary, and a writer's shed with a view. If you do a lesson on the opening, "To begin at the beginning", you might ask your students to listen to the poetry of it before they analyse it. It is a text that rewards being read aloud, and that is an area where you have the advantage of a lovely ear.

Next, two more texts from the 2027 list, both seen through live performance. Florida Weekly has a piece headlined on love and deception in The Rivals. The text is short, so it may be a review or a feature on Sheridan's comedy, but the headline gives a theme that fits the play well. Mistaken identities, romantic fictions and performed selves are all there, and for a seconde or première class they are an accessible way in to a play from the eighteenth century. A good question might be: who in the play is deceiving whom, and who is deceiving themselves? Lydia Languish, who wants her love to be as dramatic as a novel, is a rather nice figure for students who themselves enjoy stories. And there is a practical note on Twelfth Night. Chatham High School's theatre is staging it from the nineteenth to the twenty-first of November. I have no further detail on the production, but I do like the notion of a school production for a school audience. It is a reminder that this play has been taught and performed by teenagers for a very long time, and your own students might enjoy hearing that other teenagers are putting on the same play this very week. Perhaps they could think about which scenes a school cast would find hardest, or funniest, and why.

Now to the oral themes, where there are a few author-centred stories. The first is a Times of India piece on Maya Angelou and her habit of renting hotel rooms in order to write. The headline calls it an unusual routine to help her concentrate. For I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings, this is a charming bit of author context. A writer who removes herself from home, to a plain room, in order to work on a book about growing up, about voice and about silence. I think it might work as a classroom hook. You could start by asking students where they would go to write if they had to, and what the setting would do to their writing, and then lead into the book. It makes the writing of a memoir feel like a task done by a real person with a real routine, which is not always obvious to sixteen-year-olds.

There are three Atwood-adjacent or adaptation items too. The Miami Herald reports that Jess Gibson, Margaret Atwood's daughter, spoke about her first book in conversation with her mother at the Miami Book Fair. The text is brief, so I can't say much about what they discussed, but for a teacher of The Handmaid's Tale it offers a rare angle on Atwood as a mother and as a writer in a literary family. Then there is a review from Sesaya Arts Magazine of King Theatre Company's stage production of Alias Grace, Atwood's novel about Grace Marks. The reviewer says the production makes room for uncertainty, which is exactly the right instinct for that story, since the whole point of Grace is that we are never quite sure what to believe. I mention it because it is a good example of the question of how a stage version handles an unreliable, historically grounded narrator. A novel can keep a voice inside a head. A stage has to put a body in front of us. That could be a good comparison for students who are studying The Handmaid's Tale, where Offred's voice is also a reconstructed, uncertain testimony. You could ask what is gained, and what is lost, when a narrator we can only hear becomes someone we can see.

And then there is a lovely one for Atonement. IndulgExpress writes about the green gown worn in the film, and how it was designed to symbolise envy and longing. I realise film news is not your first love, but this one is really about symbolism, and so it is about the novel too. Colour as meaning, an object carrying emotion that the characters cannot say. For McEwan's text, it opens the question of how images work in the book. What does a dress do in a scene? What does the reader notice that a character does not? It is a nice bridge too, if you ever want to talk about visual art and literature together, since a costume is a kind of painting that moves.

To close, three items on reading and the craft of fiction. The Irish Independent interviews the Chinese-born American novelist Yiyun Li, who says she reads War and Peace and Moby-Dick every year, and has done so for nearly twenty years. I rather love that. It is a quiet argument for rereading, for the idea that a great book is not something one finishes but something one returns to and finds changed, because one has changed oneself. If you want a small project for your students, you could ask them to choose one text from the programme and write a note to their future self about what they hope to notice on a second reading. It could be a nice piece to revisit in terminale.

Times Now has an article on the debate about whether literary fiction needs to be realistic, prompted by a Booker Prize victory. All I have is the headline and a short summary, so I can't tell you which side it takes. But the question is a rich one for a class on narrators. Think of the books on your oral list: The Handmaid's Tale, Never Let Me Go, Parable of the Sower. Each of them bends reality, and each of them seems to tell a truth about it. Is a story less honest because it invents a future, or more? That could make a lively debate for première students, and the Booker news gives it a current hook.

And a last small mention. The Guardian has a review of One for Sorrow by Favel Parrett, with a headline calling it an affecting novel that builds to a devastating climax. I have only the headline, so I cannot say more, but I wanted you to know it is there, in case you like the sound of it for your own reading.

That is the round-up for today, Yamuna. I hope your day is as full of good stories as this one.

france.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. Today's France briefing runs from the stars to the schoolyard, with a few quieter pleasures along the way.

Let me start with the good news, which is a long way from Earth. The European Space Agency has published its first large release of images and data from the Euclid telescope, which was launched in 2023. Franceinfo reports that the pictures show hundreds of millions of galaxies. It is the sort of story that makes the ceiling of the classroom feel a little higher.

From the heavens to the dining table, The Guardian has dug out an archive piece from the eleventh of November, 1976. It describes five British chefs cooking a lunch at Maxim's in Paris, part of the long-running rivalry between British and French cooking. It is witty and richly written, and a window onto a vanished dining world. The Local France, meanwhile, has two small language nuggets. The expression of the day is "tu parles", which is not a plain statement but a retort, signalling scepticism or irony, rather like an English "yeah, right". And the word of the day is "lacrymo", the slang for tear gas, which has been much discussed in France lately.

On the weather, Storm Charles has crossed from Portugal, where it brought heavy rain and a request that people stay indoors, and it reached southern France on Thursday. On the Côte d'Azur, franceinfo reports traffic jams, a road accident, landslides and other disruption. It is not close to Grenoble, but the message from the forecasters was to stay vigilant, so it is worth a glance at the forecast if you are travelling south. Still on travel, The Local France has accounts from several British travellers who were wrongly accused of overstaying the European Union's ninety-day allowance during the chaotic start of the new biometric border checks, known as EES. If you or your British-section colleagues are planning trips, keep your travel records handy.

Now to schools, where it has been a tense few days. The Ministry of National Education reports three hoax bomb alerts, at schools in the Bouches-du-Rhône, the Aisne and the Jura, including the Lycée Don Bosco in Marseille, the university technology institute in Laon, and schools in Morez. They were false alarms, but disruptive all the same. In Paris, franceinfo has been talking to lycée head teachers about the blockades disrupting their schools. Two of them call the situation "untenable", and one asks, "how do you expect us to catch up on this?" The head teachers' union, SNPDEN-Unsa, has called on principals to gather outside their schools today, Friday, at three o'clock. Alongside this, the teaching unions are angry after Sébastien Lecornu spoke of the "complicity" of some education staff in the violence during the recent lycée protests. It is a political row, but it bears directly on school life, so I mention it for that reason.

On health, there are two stories that fit together. The government plans to put seventy new medical buses on the road, raising the number to one hundred by the end of 2027, to serve rural areas short of doctors. And franceinfo takes stock of the 2025 plan against so-called medical deserts, under which GPs were asked to spend a few days a month in underserved areas. More than six million people in France have no regular GP, and the piece asks how the scheme is working a year and a half on. For a village like yours in the Belledonne foothills, it is a story with real everyday meaning.

Today is also the thirteenth of November, and across Paris there are ceremonies marking the attacks of 2015, held at the sites where they happened. This evening, the association Life for Paris invites the public to a citizen tribute at the 13-Novembre memorial garden, to remember all victims of terrorism.

One more human piece, from franceinfo. The journalist Tristan Waleckx spent forty-eight hours in the northern neighbourhoods of Marseille, sharing residents' daily lives. The headline quotes one voice: young people from working-class neighbourhoods "do not have the right to make mistakes". It is a portrait rather than an argument, and it might stay with you.

Finally, La Mire's daily television zapping for the twelfth of November. It takes in the Armistice commemoration, an anniversary segment on Verdun, and a history teacher in the Aisne. It is quick and light, though a few segments touch on politics, so skip those if you wish.

That is France for this morning, and I hope your Friday has a little more starlight than storm in it.
france.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. Here is your gentle round-up of France for the last two days, with a solemn note at the start, a good deal about schools, and some lovely things to finish on.

Today is Friday the thirteenth of November, and it is the anniversary of the Paris attacks of 2015, eleven years on. Franceinfo explains how the day of remembrance will unfold. Commemorative ceremonies are being held at the sites of the attacks themselves, so the places where people were killed become, for a few hours, places of quiet gathering. In the evening, an association called Life for Paris is inviting the public to a citizen tribute at the 13-Novembre memorial garden. The idea is to remember all victims of terrorism, not only those of that one night. It is an open invitation, a simple gesture of standing together, and it may be a day when you find yourself thinking of the pupils who were not yet born, or were very small, when it happened.

On to the weather, because the south of France has had a wet and windy couple of days. Storm Charles first hit Portugal, where it left heavy rain and residents were urged to stay indoors. Franceinfo reported that it was expected to reach southern France on Thursday the twelfth, with officials saying, in the phrase of the headline, that people would need to stay vigilant. And it did arrive. Franceinfo describes heavy rain on the Côte d'Azur on Thursday, with traffic jams, a road accident, landslides and other disruption. None of this is close to Grenoble, so you needn't change your plans in Belledonne on its account, but if you have friends or family along the Mediterranean coast, it may be worth a message to check that their journeys are going smoothly. The advice from the authorities is the same for everyone in the storm's path: take care, be patient on the roads, and keep an eye on the local forecast.

Now to schools, where there is quite a lot to tell, and I will keep it factual. The main thread is the recent unrest in the lycées. Franceinfo has a piece in which Paris headteachers describe their despair as blockades disrupt their schools. One of them asks, "How do you expect us to catch up on this?", which rather captures the worry about lost teaching time. Two of the heads interviewed call the situation untenable. It gives a view of the crisis from the inside, from the people who have to hold a school together, keep pupils safe, and still think about timetables and exams. The head teachers' union, SNPDEN-Unsa, has called on principals to gather outside their schools today, Friday, at three in the afternoon. So if you see images of heads standing outside lycée gates this afternoon, that is what it is.

There is also a flare-up of words around all this. Franceinfo reports that teaching unions are angry after the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, spoke of the "complicity" of some Éducation nationale staff during the violence in the lycées. The unions have reacted furiously. It is a political row, and I will not dwell on it, but I mention it because it touches the daily life of the profession you work in, and it may well come up in the staffroom.

A smaller piece of school news, and a worrying one for those it affects. The Ministry of National Education has announced three hoax bomb alerts, at schools in three départements: the Bouches-du-Rhône, the Aisne and the Jura. The places named include the Lycée Don Bosco in Marseille, the IUT in Laon, and schools in Morez. They were false alarms, which is the important thing, but they still mean evacuations, disrupted lessons and some anxious hours for pupils and staff. Morez is up in the Jura, so not far from your part of the world in the grand scheme of things, though nothing suggests any link to Grenoble.

Let me turn from schools to health, where there are two connected stories about access to doctors in places where they are scarce. The Local France reports that the government plans to deploy seventy new medical buses in rural France, bringing the total to one hundred by the end of 2027. These are, as the name says, mobile surgeries that travel to areas short of doctors, so that someone in a small village need not drive a long way for a consultation. For anyone who lives, as you do, in a hillside commune above a valley, the idea has an obvious appeal. Distances and winding roads are part of mountain life, and a bus that comes to you is a practical and rather charming answer.

The second piece, from franceinfo, steps back to ask how the wider effort is going. In 2025 a plan was launched against so-called medical deserts, under which GPs were asked to spend a few days each month working in underserved areas. More than six million people in France have no regular GP, which is a striking number, and the article asks what the scheme has achieved a year and a half on. It is a story with a policy edge, but at heart it is about ordinary people trying to find someone to look after them when they are ill, and it explains why the medical buses are being expanded.

For something more human and less statistical, franceinfo has a portrait from Marseille. The journalist Tristan Waleckx spent forty-eight hours in the northern neighbourhoods of the city, the quartiers nord, and shares the daily lives of the residents he met. The headline quotes one of them: young people from these working-class neighbourhoods, it says, do not have the right to make a mistake. It is not a political argument so much as a way of listening, and I think it is the kind of reporting that a teacher of literature might appreciate, since it is built on voices and particular lives rather than generalities. If you are looking for a narrator's voice, there are some here, even if they are not in a novel.

On travel, a practical item for anyone in the British section planning a trip. The Local France reports on several British travellers who say they were wrongly accused of overstaying the European Union's ninety-day allowance. This happened during the chaotic start of the new EES biometric border checks, the system that registers travellers' entries and exits electronically. The travellers describe being caught up in confusion, and the point of the article is that the new system's early days have been rough, with mistakes that fell on the people passing through. If you or colleagues are taking pupils or families across borders in the coming months, it is worth keeping a note of your dates and being patient at the desk.

Now for some pure delight. The European Space Agency has published the first large release of images and data from its Euclid telescope, which was launched in 2023. Franceinfo reports that the pictures show hundreds of millions of galaxies. It is hard to imagine a number like that, hundreds of millions of galaxies, each of them containing countless stars, and yet here they are, photographed. It is one of those stories that reaches well beyond France and reminds us how much there is out there. If you ever want a way into a lesson on awe, on the sublime as the Romantic poets understood it, this would make a lovely starting point, a modern answer to Wordsworth and Keats looking up at the sky.

And from the heavens back to Paris, and to a very different sort of wonder, a delicious piece from the archive of The Guardian. It dates from the eleventh of November 1976, and describes five British chefs cooking a lunch at Maxim's in Paris, against the background of the old culinary rivalry between Britain and France. The headline says the rivalry is heating up, and the pun is surely intended. What makes it a pleasure is the prose: witty, richly written, with the confidence of a newspaper from another era. It is also a window onto a vanished dining world, with its own manners and its own assumptions. I thought of you at once, because it reads almost like a scene from a comic novel, with the chefs as characters in their own right, the great restaurant as stage and the rivalry as plot.

Since you teach English to French pupils, here are two small language nuggets from The Local France. The first is the expression of the day: "Tu parles !" It is a retort that signals scepticism or irony, rather than just stating the obvious. So when someone says "Tu parles !", they usually mean something like "Yeah, right!" or "You must be joking." It is a good one to set beside English equivalents, and to show pupils how tone can overturn the literal sense of words, a lesson as useful for reading Austen's irony as for chatting in a café.

The second is the word of the day: "lacrymo," the slang abbreviation for tear gas, from "lacrymogène." It has been much discussed in France recently, which is why it is in the news. The piece itself is quite short, but it is a nice example of how French likes to clip its words into friendly little forms, even for rather unfriendly things.

Finally, La Mire's daily video, the zapping of French television, for the twelfth of November. This edition covers the Armistice commemoration, an anniversary segment connected with Verdun, and a history teacher in the Aisne. It is quick and light, and a handy way to see what French television has been showing, though a few of the segments do touch on politics, so you can skip those if you prefer. The history teacher is a nice thread for you, since the video sets a classroom beside the great memories of the First World War.

That is France for today. I hope your Friday is dry, your lessons calm, and that somewhere between Les Adrets and the valley you find a good cup of something warm.

Good morning, Yamuna. Today's good news is full of things hidden in plain sight, finally found or finally seen, with a few small kindnesses alongside.

Let me begin with books, since the literary world has had a lovely week. M John Harrison has become the oldest person ever to win the Booker Prize, at eighty-one. The Rugby Observer notes that he was born in Rugby, so there is local pride there too. In an interview with The Bookseller, he talks about age, writing and his long refusal of genre labels, and he says, rather wonderfully, "It's weird because I still feel twenty-six." That is a line you might happily read out to your première students. The Guardian has a thoughtful companion piece asking whether his win, the first for a novel leaning towards science fiction, means the literary establishment has finally made peace with the fantastic. Kazuo Ishiguro and others weigh in, so it could make good material for a class discussion about how prizes treat stories that don't sit neatly in the realist tradition. And since Under Milk Wood is on the 2027 session, you may like to hear that the Tenby Observer reports major investment has been secured for the Dylan Thomas Boathouse in Laugharne, the very place where he lived and wrote.

Now to art, and a run of stories about things lost and found. Good News Network reports that researchers have identified two hundred and eighty Ice Age engravings in a cave on Spain's Mediterranean coast. It is the third-largest such collection found in that region, and visitors had been walking right past the carvings for more than sixty years without noticing them. In a very different key, the same outlet tells the story of a woman called Betsy, clearing out an East Village apartment in New York. Her elderly aunt remarked, almost casually, that there was a Georgia O'Keeffe in the closet. That sentence led to the painting's rediscovery, and it's a charming reminder of how much can hang on a few spoken words. Upworthy, meanwhile, has a man who went looking for a lost hammer as a favour to a friend, and instead turned up more than fifteen thousand Roman coins. The piece suggests the search mattered as history, too, not just as luck.

Closer to your own interests, Beaux Arts Magazine reports that Metz is hosting the first international retrospective of Séraphine Louis, who lived from eighteen sixty-four to nineteen forty-two. She was a self-taught painter who worked as a cleaner, and the exhibition aims to show the great painter behind the legend, an overlooked artist finally seen on her own terms. Metz is not so far away, and it might be a worthwhile trip. Also from the world of painters, Upworthy revisits Salvador Dalí's habit of napping while holding a key. As he drifted off, the key would fall, the clatter would wake him, and he would seize whatever idea was floating in that half-dreaming state. Scientists now think he may have been onto something, which pleases me, because it suggests the surrealists were running experiments as much as playing games.

On to people, and some warm stories about generosity and memory. Good News Network tells of Bonnie Fay, who is eighty-four and plays the piano. Years ago she was a patient at Bryn Mawr Village nursing home in Pennsylvania, recovering from Guillain-Barré syndrome, a condition that left her paralysed. She has now returned to the same home to play for the residents, giving back the music that helped her through. The same outlet reports on a one-hundred-and-three-year-old D-Day veteran who has been reunited with his lost war medals, in time for Remembrance Day. An amateur historian of the Second World War traced him through his military record and brought them home. It is a quiet, moving story about how memory can be kept alive by patient, unglamorous work.

There are two gentler stories too. In Bradley, Illinois, Gretchen Sollo turned one hundred. She walks through her local Lowe's store every day, and the staff who see her there organised her first ever surprise birthday party. Good News Network calls her the store's mom, and it sounds as though she has earned the title. And from Positivr, a small act of care in Cuincy, near Lille. A florist who would otherwise throw away her unsold chrysanthemums after All Saints' has been placing them on forgotten graves in the cemetery, so that people with no one left to visit them are remembered too. It is a modest gesture, but a deeply humane one.

Finally, two stories for nature and for the future. Good News Network reports that Cantabrian brown bears in Spain have roughly doubled in number over the past twenty years, from as few as one hundred and forty to about three hundred and seventy. They are also now living across a much wider area, which is a concrete and encouraging conservation result. And Reasons to be Cheerful, together with the Outrider Foundation, offers a more dreamlike idea. It looks back to twenty twelve, when Philip Wallisfurth proposed using moss to help save a hundred-and-fifty-year-old tree in Aachen, and it imagines mossier, greener cities of the future. It is the kind of gentle, inventive thinking that feels almost like a short story waiting to be written.

That is all for today, Yamuna, and I hope something in it turns up, like a Roman coin, exactly where you least expected it.
