Good morning, Yamuna. Today's good news has a lot of hidden things coming into the light, from painted caves to forgotten graves, and a few late bloomers who are finally getting their due.

Let me begin with books, because the literary world has had a cheering couple of days. M John Harrison has won the Booker Prize at the age of eighty-one, which makes him the oldest winner in the prize's history. The Rugby Observer is proud to note that he was born in Rugby, and describes it as a heartening story of late recognition. The Bookseller has an interview with him in which he talks about age, writing, and his long refusal of genre labels. His line about it is rather lovely: "It's weird because I still feel twenty-six." There's something disarming about hearing that from a man who has just made Booker history, and it might be a nice thing to read out to a class who assume that writers are born venerable.

The Guardian, meanwhile, asks a bigger question. Harrison's win is the first for a novel leaning towards science fiction, so does it mean a snobbish literary establishment has finally accepted the genre? Kazuo Ishiguro is among those who weigh in. It's a useful piece on how prizes have treated the fantastic over the years, and it could make a good starting point for a discussion with your première students about what we mean by literary fiction in the first place, and who gets to decide.

Staying with writers, there is a piece of cultural good news from south-west Wales. The Tenby Observer reports that major investment has been secured for the Dylan Thomas Boathouse in Laugharne. With Under Milk Wood on the twenty twenty-seven session, it feels like a timely piece of news. That poet's house above the estuary, with all that musical language poured out of it, is going to be looked after properly.

Now to art, and to the pleasure of things hidden in plain sight. The Good News Network tells of a cave on Spain's Mediterranean coast where researchers have found two hundred and eighty Ice Age engravings. It's the third-largest collection of its kind found there. The remarkable detail is that visitors had been walking past these engravings for more than sixty years without seeing them. Think of that: the oldest images we know, made by human hands, and generations of people strolling by in the half-dark, looking straight at them. It says something about how seeing is a skill, and how much of it is simply knowing how to look. That is surely one of the first lessons of reading, too.

A rather more recent rediscovery comes from the same outlet. A woman named Betsy was clearing out an apartment in New York's East Village when her elderly aunt said something wonderfully offhand: there's a Georgia O'Keeffe in the closet. That single remark led to the painting's rediscovery. I love the way the whole thing begins with a sentence, just words spoken in passing, and it ends with a painting back in the world. It's a story that sits neatly between the two things you care about, painting and the spoken or written word.

There is another painter to tell you about, this one in France. Beaux Arts Magazine reports that the first international retrospective of Séraphine Louis is opening in Metz. She lived from eighteen sixty-four to nineteen forty-two, taught herself to paint, and worked as a cleaner. The legend around her has long been that of the naive visionary, and the exhibition aims to show the great painter behind that legend. I find that very moving, because it's about an artist being seen on her own terms rather than through the story that other people told about her. If you fancy a day trip east, and with a lycée timetable you may not, it sounds worth putting on a list. It would also pair beautifully with a lesson on how biographies and myths can shape, and sometimes shrink, an artist.

And then a sideways link between painting and the mind. Upworthy writes about Salvador Dalí's peculiar habit of napping while holding a key. As he drifted off, the key would slip from his fingers, hit the floor and wake him, ideally with a fresh idea still clinging to him from the edge of sleep. For years it has seemed like one of those surreal anecdotes that belongs more to Dalí's persona than to anything real. Now scientists think he may well have been onto something. It's a charming connection between art, creativity and sleep research, and I can imagine it being a good opening for a creative writing session: a few minutes of drifting, a pencil in hand, and see what comes.

Staying with lucky finds, Upworthy also has a story of a man who went looking for a lost hammer and found more than fifteen thousand Roman coins instead. The text is short, but the outline is delightful. It began as a favour for a friend, and it ended as a piece of history coming up out of the ground. Fifteen thousand coins is a vast number, and it's one of those stories that makes you look at every ordinary field a little differently.

Let me turn now to music, memory and small acts of kindness, because several of today's stories belong together. The first is from the Good News Network, about Bonnie Fay, an eighty-four-year-old piano player in Pennsylvania. Some time ago she was a patient at the Bryn Mawr Village nursing home, after Guillain-Barré syndrome left her paralysed. Now she returns there to play for the residents, giving music back to the place that cared for her. It's a story about recovery, but also about generosity, and the idea that what we are given can be handed on. I think you'd enjoy the image of her at the keys, in a room where people once wondered whether she would play again.

The same outlet brings another story about memory, this time on a larger scale. A one-hundred-and-three-year-old D-Day veteran has been reunited with his war medals, returned in time for Remembrance Day. An amateur historian of the Second World War traced him through his military record, patiently following the paperwork back to the man. It is a quiet story, and the sort in which history is not a date in a textbook but a person who is still here to receive what he earned. You often say that novels teach history better than essays, and this is the real-life version: the great events narrowed down to one man, one set of medals, and someone who cared enough to find him.

Then a gentler tale from Bradley, Illinois. Gretchen Sollo turned one hundred, and the staff at the Lowe's store where she takes her daily walks gave her a surprise party, the first birthday party she has ever had. The Good News Network calls her the store mom, which tells you how long she has been part of the place. It has the lightness and the quiet humanity of a short story, an ordinary setting suddenly full of warmth, and a character you would happily follow for a chapter or two.

And a moving one from closer to home. Positivr tells of a florist in Cuincy, near Lille, who would otherwise throw away her unsold flowers after All Saints'. Instead, she lays them on the forgotten graves in the cemetery, the ones that nobody has visited. There is no grand scheme, no campaign, just a woman with leftover flowers and an eye for the graves that have no one to bring any. It's an elegant answer to waste and to loneliness at the same time, and I think it would sit well beside a poem about remembrance.

Finally, two stories about the living world. First, a real conservation success. The Good News Network reports that the Cantabrian brown bear population in Spain has roughly doubled over the last twenty years, from as few as one hundred and forty animals to about three hundred and seventy. They are also living across a much wider area than before. That's what matters here: it's not simply a count that has risen, but a range that has opened up again, so the bears have more country to move through. It is a concrete outcome after decades of effort, which is precisely what we look for in good news.

And last, something hopeful and inventive, from Reasons to be Cheerful, published together with the Outrider Foundation. The piece is about Philip Wallisfurth, who in twenty twelve proposed using moss as a way to save a one-hundred-and-fifty-year-old tree in Aachen. From that idea, the article imagines the mossy cities of the future, greener and softer than the ones we know. I like the thought of a city that is gradually clothed in something old and quiet and living. It reads a little like the opening of a utopian novel, though this one starts with a real tree and a real man with an idea.

That's the news for today, and I hope some of it follows you up the hill to Les Adrets: perhaps a key in the hand at nap time, or at least a closer look at whatever you pass by on the way.

It's told through the voices of ordinary civilians around the world, in Germany, Russia and Singapore among other places, in the year the war became truly global. It has a polyphonic quality, almost like a novel with many narrators, which I think you'll appreciate. Sticking with history, there's a documentary on Emil Jellinek, called Monsieur Mercedes: la naissance d'une étoile. Jellinek was the Austro-Hungarian consul in Nice and a passionate motoring enthusiast, and he founded the Mercedes brand in nineteen-oh-two. It's told as a story of people rather than industry, which makes it far more inviting than it sounds.

It begins in eighteen ninety-three, with the opening of the Hôtel Tassel in Brussels, and follows Horta's use of iron, glass and light as the style spread across Europe. It's a lovely companion for anyone drawn to the Belle Époque, and perhaps a thought for a classroom conversation about how paintings and writing of that era shared a sensibility.

It runs at the Royal Opera House in London from the twenty-second of February to the thirteenth of March, twenty twenty-seven. The Guardian's film critic, who co-wrote the thriller Hunting Alice Bell, has gone into a TV writers' room and talked with showrunners, including Jesse Armstrong of Succession, about the craft. The headline quotes one of them saying it's like having your brain squeezed, which tells you something about the pressure and intensity involved. For someone who spends time thinking about how stories are built, it sounds like a good read, and perhaps useful material to bring to older students who are curious about how a narrative gets made by a group rather than a single author.

So if I had to pick for the weekend, I'd start with La Chimère on Arte, then the Horta documentary for something beautiful, and keep the MADDADDAM trailer for a quiet moment with a cup of tea.

Enjoy it all, Yamuna, and may your evenings be well supplied with good stories.

briefing.text:
Good morning, Yamuna, and happy Friday.

Let me begin with books. The Bookseller has an interview with M John Harrison, at eighty-one the oldest person ever to win the Booker Prize. He talks about age, about writing, and about his long refusal to be pinned down by genre labels. His line is wonderfully candid: "It's weird because I still feel twenty-six." It might be a nice thing to read out to your students, who may be surprised to hear that the feeling of being young doesn't necessarily leave.

In The Guardian, there's a review of the audiobook of Ben Lerner's Transcription, narrated by Seth Numrich. An anxious, unnamed narrator travels to interview his former mentor, a ninety-year-old German writer, and the story becomes a layered meditation on memory, family and storytelling. The reviewer calls it a book for the smartphone era, and it sounds as though the voice does a great deal of the work.

Now to the arts, where several stories talk to one another. On Radio 4's Front Row, there's a review of Jonathan Coe's novel Lessons in Harmony, which imagines the friendship between Ravel and Vaughan Williams. The same programme looks at Inside Bloomsbury, the Tate Britain exhibition on Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant, and also at the Palme d'Or winner, Fjord. Fiction, music and painting in one sitting.

In Metz, the first international retrospective of Séraphine Louis, who lived from eighteen sixty-four to nineteen forty-two, has opened. Beaux Arts Magazine says it reveals the great painter behind the legend: a self-taught artist who worked as a cleaner, and who is now being seen on her own terms. It's a story that already feels like a novel.

And a very different way of looking at a famous painting. Hyperallergic reports that scientists have found Rembrandt's Night Watch is home to teeming microbes, an invisible world living on the canvas. They hope it may help explain some of the painting's mysteries. It's a rather lovely thought that a picture four centuries old is, quite literally, alive.

Closer to home, l'Essentiel announces a new exhibition at the Musée de Grenoble. I'm afraid all we have is the headline, so the artists, dates and themes remain a mystery, but it may be worth a look at the museum's own pages.

Now for some good news. Good News Network tells the story of a woman called Betsy, who was clearing out an East Village apartment with her elderly aunt when the aunt remarked, almost in passing, that there was a Georgia O'Keeffe in the closet. Those few words led to the painting's joyous rediscovery. It's a reminder of how a single sentence can change the fate of a work of art.

The same site has a quieter, more moving story. A one hundred and three-year-old D-Day veteran has been reunited with the war medals he had lost. An amateur historian of the Second World War traced him through his military record, and the medals reached him in time for Remembrance Day.

On to your BFI corner. The Tenby Observer reports that major investment has been secured for the Dylan Thomas Boathouse in Laugharne. With Under Milk Wood on the twenty twenty-seven programme, it's a welcome piece of cultural news from south-west Wales. And from The Guardian, Alexis Petridis reviews Hamlet Hail to the Thief, a mash-up of Shakespeare and Radiohead. He finds it rotten in places, to borrow a Danish phrase, but ultimately redeeming, and he calls the album Radiohead's "record that got away". Given that Hamlet is on the seconde and première programme, it may be a curious way to introduce it.

Now, around you. Grenoble Mag says the organist Michel Alleysson is setting Bach in conversation with Italian music at the Saint-Joseph organ in Grenoble. The piece gives no date, but it sounds like exactly the kind of recital you enjoy in a local church.

France 3 Alpes has a story from Isère that reads almost like historical fiction. A woman, the great-granddaughter of a poilu who was interned in a psychiatric hospital after the Great War, is writing to give him back his voice. The title quotes a phrase of the time: "men suffering from women's illnesses". It's a story of family history and of the forgotten psychological toll of nineteen fourteen to eighteen.

History comes to the screen too. ARTE has a documentary, 1942: un monde en guerre, covering January to May, the months when the war became truly global. It's told through the voices of civilians in Germany, Russia, Singapore and elsewhere, a polyphonic account that may appeal to you as someone who prefers history through stories.

Today in France is also a day of remembrance. It's the anniversary of the thirteenth of November attacks in Paris in twenty fifteen, and commemorative ceremonies are taking place at the sites of the attacks. This evening, the association Life for Paris invites the public to a citizen tribute at the memorial garden, to remember all victims of terrorism.

Franceinfo also offers a human portrait from Marseille. The journalist Tristan Waleckx spent forty-eight hours in the northern neighbourhoods, sharing residents' daily lives. The headline quotes a resident saying that young people there have no right to make mistakes.

And to end on something to watch tonight. Arte is showing La Chimère, in which Josh O'Connor plays a man who plunders Etruscan tombs in search of a lost love. It's a romantic, archaeological premise, and a rather dreamlike one.

That's your Daily Yam for today, Yamuna, and I hope your Friday is full of good stories and a little music.
